en: Heating solid ice adds energy, causing its water molecules to vibrate faster and break their rigid bonds to form liquid water.
When warm, moist air touches a cold glass, the air cools down and its water vapor loses energy to become liquid droplets.
Mixing baking soda and vinegar causes an acid-base reaction that rapidly produces carbon dioxide gas, creating the visible fizzing bubbles.
Exposing iron to oxygen and liquid water causes a chemical reaction that slowly transforms the metal into flaky, reddish-brown iron oxide rust.
Stirring sugar into warm water causes the fast-moving water molecules to pull individual sugar molecules apart, forming a clear, uniform solution.
Heating a saltwater solution causes the liquid water to evaporate into gas, leaving the solid salt crystals behind in the container.
Pouring vegetable oil into water causes the oil to float on top because its molecules are packed less densely than water molecules.
Heating a tightly closed metal jar lid causes its metal atoms to move faster and spread apart, making the lid expand and loosen.
Pumping air into a flat bicycle tire forces more gas molecules into a small space, increasing pressure to make the tire firm.
Pouring muddy water through filter paper causes the tiny liquid water molecules to pass through, while trapping the larger solid dirt particles.
Placing liquid water in a freezer removes thermal energy, causing the molecules to slow down and lock into a rigid, solid ice structure.
Touching a hot metal spoon transfers thermal energy quickly to your hand because its tightly packed atoms easily pass vibrating energy to each other.
